title: Western Pacific volume gave no clear six-month ENSO uncertainty forecast gain beyond season and temperature in 2000-2024
abstract: We tested whether western Pacific warm water volume improved six-month ENSO error variance forecasts beyond season and current Nino 3.4 temperature. Frozen NOAA GODAS and ERSSTv5 data supplied 300 monthly forecast origins in 2000-2024. Mean and variance fits used earlier targets only. Adding signed western volume raised mean Gaussian negative log density from 0.94680 to 0.95245 nats. Reference-minus-test gain was -0.00564 nats, with a conditional 95% three-year block interval of -0.01254 to +0.00022. Five-year blocks and a mean model with western volume also gave no clear signed-volume gain. An absolute-volume check gave no clear gain with the main mean model and worse scores with the larger mean model. These results bound the tested statistical method. They do not reject physical changes in ENSO noise or the value of ocean heat content in other models. Few ENSO cycles, revised data, Gaussian errors and fixed model forms limit the result. Original code, aggregate evidence, a figure, hashes and external retrieval instructions support reproduction.

display.caption: Western volume gave no clear signed-volume score gain. Positive gains mean smaller density loss. Limits use paired three-year blocks of origin years. The larger mean model also uses western volume.

citations.reason: We extend its earlier-error calibration design and fixed mean-model specification with a new western-volume variance test. Code is written anew; the basin and temperature inputs overlap.
Its seasonal uncertainty benchmark motivates controlling for season before testing volume.
Planton and coauthors (2021) study asymmetric heat-content effects on ENSO predictability in model ensembles. Our statistical error-variance test has a different scope.
